ety.text: From English dialectal hyke (“to walk vigorously”), probably a Northern form of hitch, from Middle English hytchen, hichen, icchen (“to move, jerk, stir”). Cognate with Scots hyke (“to move with a jerk”), dialectal German hicken (“to hobble, walk with a limp”), Danish hinke (“to hop”).

senses.d: A long walk, usually for pleasure or exercise.
ex: From here, you can pick up the asphalt bike path and take a hike across the meadow.
The hike through the city of Napa's Alston Park is a great introduction to the Napa Valley.
The tenants were not happy with the rent hike.

senses.d: The snap of the ball to start a play.
A sharp upward tug to raise something.
ex: She gave a cute hike of her skirt as she spun and almost sauntered down the stairs.

senses.d: To take a long walk (on something) for pleasure or exercise.
ex: Don't forget to bring the map when we go hiking tomorrow.
When Dick Hudson hiked the trail between 1966 and 1970, he met so few hikers that he can still recall nearly all of them.

senses.d: To unfairly or suddenly raise a price.
To snap the ball to start a play.
To lean out to the windward side of a sailboat in order to counterbalance the effects of the wind on the sails.
To pull up or tug upwards sharply.
Let's go; get moving. A command to a dog sled team, given by a musher.
